positive: She felt uncomfortable being in the spotlight.
The actor has remained in the public eye for years.
A newly reported scientist is in the public eye.
negative: The actor is in the public eyes.
The committee quietly discussed it with no public attention.
proposals.meaningImpact: Canonical 116 already means public attention; add media-visible/famous public-eye usage as a near-synonymous lexical form. Never teach a mandatory brief-versus-long duration divide: Cambridge gives years in the spotlight.

contentPlan.change: Present in the spotlight / in the public eye as two public-attention forms; note public-eye often describes well-known, media-visible people. Preserve that attention may be welcome or unwelcome.
Replace one target-bearing key with an actor or public advocate widely covered in media, using in the public eye; keep facts sufficient for public visibility, not a single private compliment.
Use in the public eye in a new speech line and explanatory takeaway so the additional form is assessed and has a prerecorded model; update exact target span and audio request.

Rewrite the new-context prompt and one model for sustained public visibility and interview boundaries; keep the other model in the spotlight for a recent attention event; recalculate answer-derived glossary spans and EN/ZH.

proposals.boundary: Neither phrase alone proves fame is liked, nor does duration alone distinguish them.
proposals.sourceExample: The actor has remained in the public eye for years.

positive: The committee remained stuck in old patterns.
A team can become trapped in old habits.
We are trapped in old habits of choosing the same speakers.
negative: A team is trapped in a cycle of debt.
The committee deliberately kept a proven method after review.
proposals.meaningImpact: Canonical 549 already teaches repeated familiar behaviour that blocks needed change. Trapped in old habits adds a natural surface image, not a new behavioural outcome; avoid converting all old habits into defects.

contentPlan.change: Add trapped in old habits as an alternative construction alongside stuck in old patterns, with be/become/get and a concrete repeated behaviour.
Use trapped in old habits as a target-bearing keyed answer in one existing committee/friend scenario, ensuring the prompt shows repetition and resistance to a needed change.
Include the alternate form in an audio-backed model and takeaway, with exact target span; keep the practical small-change learner outcome.
Retain the original new-context writing decision, but use trapped in old habits in one full model and stuck in old patterns in the other; refresh Chinese and answer-derived glossary offsets.

proposals.boundary: Unlike old habits die hard, the learner must identify a limiting repeated practice, not just observe that habit change can be difficult.
proposals.sourceExample: A team can become trapped in old habits.

positive: Getting support will be an uphill battle.
High rent can make saving feel like an endless uphill climb.
Saving for the move has been an uphill climb.
negative: The road has an uphill slope.
One routine request was accepted immediately.
proposals.meaningImpact: Canonical 100 covers sustained effort against obstacles and even includes affordable-housing source examples. Uphill climb uses journey imagery but source supplies the same saving/housing difficulty; endless adds emphasis without a new lesson outcome.

contentPlan.change: Add an uphill climb, optionally endless, as a second effort metaphor; keep outcome uncertainty and avoid literal-slope interpretation.
Add one target-bearing uphill-climb example in a genuinely new task (e.g. long-term repayment under rising fees), while preserving one uphill-battle item.
Demonstrate both expressions across the two takeaways or speaking model and validate the new audio target span.
One model may use an uphill climb and one an uphill battle for the same difficult community project, retaining exact obstacles and proposed first steps; recalculate glossary and Chinese.

proposals.boundary: Do not claim climb guarantees gradual progress or battle necessarily means opponents; both can mark difficult prolonged effort.
proposals.sourceExample: High rent can make saving feel like an endless uphill climb.
